candidates.text:
BREAKING: We just sued Amazon over what we believe was a vast, ad-rigging scheme.

We believe Amazon found a way to charge a few extra pennies to an enormous number of transactions, adding up to over $20 billion in illegal charges.

This is about how something becomes a "Sponsored product."

Amazon lets businesses bid to be "Sponsored" but it told businesses that the highest bid would only pay slightly more than the second-highest bid.

For example: If you bid $1 to have your product “Sponsored” and the next-highest bid is $0.50, you should pay about $0.51.

But we believe that Amazon would run the auction, see those bids, and then secretly raise the second-place price so it could charge the winner more.

It was a gradual strategy based on concealment.

Internal Amazon documents show they tested how much they could raise those hidden charges without advertisers catching on, then raised them more when businesses didn’t react, then gave false answers when businesses started asking questions.

This is a case about affordability, fair competition, and basic honesty in the marketplace. My thanks to the big bipartisan team on this, from AGs across the country to the FTC.

candidates.text:
We’re hiring experienced Product Managers to join us at @Rippling in Bangalore - Roles open for Lead PMs (7+ years) and Staff PMs (9+ years).

One of the things that makes product management at Rippling interesting is the shape and scale of the company. Payroll, Benefits, Recruiting, Time, Expenses, IT, Identity, Procurement, Travel, Corporate cards, SOC2  - many of these could be billion dollar standalone software companies. However, at Rippling, they’re products built on the same platform, sharing the same employee data and increasingly being orchestrated by Rippling AI.

That creates a different kind of PM problem. You need to understand your product deeply, but also understand the system around it. A decision in Payroll can affect Time, Benefits or Finance. A workflow that once required someone to navigate four products can potentially become one AI-driven action / automation.

The hard part is figuring out how all of this should work while keeping the experience simple.
We’re looking for PMs who like that kind of complexity - strong product thinkers who can go deep with engineering, stay close to customers, and have the judgment to turn a complicated, multi screen problem into a simple, intuitive, touch of a button.

Our business is growing ~80% YoY on a $1.2 Bn ARR and I’m certain this is a generational company in the making. 

If this sounds interesting, please reach out to me. 

RT for good karma ✌🏻

Cheers!

candidates.text:
Honest post: the Polymarket DeFi CLOB is full of tech debt. It grew fast, got hacked together, and most of the team inherited it that way. Since joining and building out the team, we have scaled it 10x and made it 3x faster, but it’s not enough; the core foundations of how it’s been built are wrong in almost every way. You try to fix one thing, and another thing goes wrong; the conclusion now is that the codebase can’t be saved long-term.

The exchange is the heart of Polymarket; everything runs through it. If we want to be the best exchange in the world, it must be fast, stable, and scalable. We can’t keep patching the old one, where these core foundations are generally missing throughout, so we’re rewriting it from scratch in Rust.

Early numbers: 10-20x faster on p99 than today, 200,000 orders per second (15x what we have now, with room to reach 400,000+), and stability under load. This will put us faster than most exchanges, including CEXs.

Building it in Rust gives us memory safety with no garbage collector. No GC means no random pauses and no random latency spikes; the tail latency in the benchmarks is the tail latency you get in production, alongside a strict compiler that enforces correctness up front. Data races and memory corruption (the bugs that take exchanges down) can’t exist in the first place.

Polymarket has to take it seriously that we are an exchange; this is people’s money, not a joke. To succeed, we have to fix this; otherwise, we will fail. It’s as simple as that. I joined to build the best software in the world, not to maintain some of the worst, and I will do everything I can to make Polymarket a serious exchange.

We are aiming to have the exchange ready sometime in Q4 (mid to end). I'll communicate progress as we go so you all know the status. Breaking changes will be minimal for all integrators and will be communicated in advance. We will maintain the existing CLOB and keep trying to improve it as we build this side by side. We can’t wait to throw away the existing CLOB; we dislike it as much as you all do.

Make Polymarket fast, finally.

interesting debate at our CAB meeting last week

Will creative continue to be the most important lever in marketing or so cheap and commoditized it stops being a lever at all?

Camp 1: Media buying, targeting, optimization, reporting - when all of it automates away with AI, what’s left for a human to actually own? Creative. It becomes the only lever that still requires taste, making it the most important one.

Camp 2: Doesn’t matter how good the idea is. The second something works, it gets copied by competitors. Creative has never been more disposable and the advantage now lasts days v quarters.

I have thought about this a great deal. Imagine a small town built entirely around research: your colleagues live nearby, there are no exhausting commutes, and everything can be reached on foot, by bicycle, or by a small shuttle. Your financial needs are taken care of, leaving you free to focus on research rather than administration. There is no teaching unless you choose to do it, and, naturally, no grant proposals.

Each researcher has a comfortable home, with enough space to raise a family and live without financial strain. Schools, cinemas, cafés, bars, grocery stores, and everyday shops are all within walking distance. Across the campus, spacious buildings house vast libraries, quiet offices, well-equipped laboratories, cafeterias, lecture halls, gardens, and welcoming communal spaces where researchers can meet, think, and exchange ideas.

Beyond the buildings are quiet parks and stretches of woodland. Whiteboards and outdoor office pods are scattered throughout the grounds, allowing people to work or discuss ideas outside whenever they wish. Bicycles and electric scooters are readily available everywhere, making it easy to move around.
